headline: Parliament Passes Major Health and Road-Safety Reforms Amid Disputes Over Rights and Public Services
summary: Parliament advanced or passed a wide range of legislation under urgency, including major changes to workplace safety, mental health care, road-use enforcement and offshore renewable energy. Government supporters said the measures would improve safety, access to services and investment, while opposition parties raised concerns about worker protections, Māori health equity, homelessness and the effects of fast-tracked lawmaking.

topicSummaries.topic: Health and Safety Bill Passes, with Changes Delayed Until April 2027
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The law changes the health and safety duties of many small businesses, potentially affecting protections for hundreds of thousands of workers.
topicSummaries.content: The Health and Safety at Work Amendment Bill passed its third reading after the Government amended its commencement date to 1 April 2027. It prioritises the management of risks likely to cause death or serious harm and gives businesses with fewer than 20 workers fewer duties for risks classed as non-critical; it also changes WorkSafe’s stated functions. Minister Brooke van Velden said the reforms would simplify compliance and focus attention on serious risks. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori argued the small-business exemption could weaken protections, while New Zealand First said it had reservations but was supporting the bill under the coalition agreement and would seek changes before implementation.

keyExchanges.speaker: Brooke van Velden (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: This bill reflects that this Government is listening to the people on the ground—the small businesses—having to deal with our laws day in and day out.

keyExchanges.speaker: Mark Patterson (NZ First)
keyExchanges.quote: It has not been possible to convince our coalition colleagues to make substantial changes, and we are compelled to vote for this bill via the coalition agreement.

topicSummaries.topic: Mental Health Bill Passes After Debate on Rights and Safeguards
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill replaces a decades-old law governing compulsory mental health care and sets rules for how people’s rights and treatment are handled.
topicSummaries.content: The Mental Health Bill passed its third reading after committee debate on compulsory care, supported decision-making, seclusion, electroconvulsive therapy and safeguards for children and other vulnerable people. The Government said the bill would create a modern, rights-based framework and make compulsory care a last resort, with a two-year implementation period. Labour and the Greens supported the bill but argued it did not go far enough on ending seclusion, resourcing services, protecting whānau involvement and strengthening rights safeguards. Opposition amendments on seclusion, whānau participation and implementation reporting were not agreed to.

keyExchanges.speaker: Matt Doocey (National)
keyExchanges.quote: This bill represents a significant step forward, modernising a system that is more than 30 years old, and bringing it up to date with how we expect mental health care to be delivered in this country.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ingrid Leary (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: We do support this bill, but we think it could have gone a lot further.

topicSummaries.topic: Homelessness and Emergency Housing Policies Face Renewed Scrutiny
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Disputes over who can access emergency accommodation affect people at immediate risk of sleeping rough and the support available to them.
topicSummaries.content: Opposition MPs challenged the Government over reports of rising homelessness and alleged that performance measures for Ministry of Social Development staff could discourage emergency housing grants. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon rejected that link and cited Government figures showing fewer households in emergency housing, more children out of motels and a decline in Auckland rough-sleeping counts. Labour and Green MPs questioned where people turned away from emergency accommodation had gone and raised concerns about access to support; the Speaker also reminded ministers to answer questions without using them to attack the Opposition. An urgent debate request on staff performance measures was declined.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Why are Ministers in his Government apparently the only people that cannot see the link between booting people out of emergency accommodation and record numbers of homeless people living rough on the streets?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: We have put $10 million of additional funding in place; we’ve had 177 enter new transitional housing; we’ve had 1,500 support activities.

topicSummaries.topic: Antisocial Road Use Bill Passes with Vehicle Forfeiture Powers
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The law gives police and courts stronger tools against dangerous street racing and related behaviour that can endanger residents, road users and officers.
topicSummaries.content: The Antisocial Road Use Legislation Amendment Bill passed its third reading with support from National, Labour, ACT and New Zealand First; the Greens opposed it. The law creates a new offence for frightening or intimidating convoys, introduces presumptive vehicle forfeiture or destruction for specified offences, expands police powers to close areas, and raises the excessive-vehicle-noise infringement fee. Labour supported the bill but questioned whether police would have enough resources to enforce it. The Greens argued that existing offences and penalties, rather than further increases, should be backed by enforcement and prevention.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Bishop (National)
keyExchanges.quote: If you choose Grand Theft Auto - style behaviour, do not be surprised when you get real-world consequences.

keyExchanges.speaker: Julie Anne Genter (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Simply changing the law and giving the police more powers and increasing penalties doesn’t address the issue because people aren’t deterred by the consequences.

topicSummaries.topic: Pae Ora Amendments Pass, Changing Health-System Governance and Targets
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The changes shape how Health New Zealand sets priorities, works with providers and addresses health needs across population groups.
topicSummaries.content: The Healthy Futures (Pae Ora) Amendment Bill passed its third reading. It adds statutory health targets, changes Health New Zealand’s governance and infrastructure arrangements, clarifies its ability to work with private providers, and requires political-neutrality principles to apply to specified Health New Zealand personnel. It also repeals the health-sector principles and charter and changes the Act’s title order. The Government said the changes would sharpen accountability and focus on patient access; Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori argued they weakened equity and Treaty-related safeguards and could discourage health workers from speaking publicly about concerns.

keyExchanges.speaker: Simeon Brown (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The Government sets the priorities, Health New Zealand delivers the care, patients feel the benefits, the public sees the results.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ayesha Verrall (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: There is so much effort to silence healthcare workers from their duty to advocate through this effort to draw them into the cloak of Public Service neutrality.

topicSummaries.topic: Offshore Renewable Energy Bill Passes with Seabed-Mining Restrictions
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The new permit system is intended to give developers clearer rights to assess offshore projects and could support future electricity supply and investment.
topicSummaries.content: The Offshore Renewable Energy Bill passed its third reading, establishing feasibility and commercial permits, decommissioning obligations and a process for ministers to designate areas where seabed-mining restrictions apply. Labour and the Greens supported the bill while criticising delays and calling for stronger engagement with iwi and hapū; the Government said the regime would provide certainty and flexibility for developers. The law covers offshore renewable sources beyond wind, although speakers said offshore wind was the principal near-term focus.

keyExchanges.speaker: Megan Woods (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: It would have been better if we’d had it sooner, but better late than never.

keyExchanges.speaker: Simon Watts (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The proposals that you have outlined would enshrine how competing uses are dealt with in the legislation and not provide flexibility for how this is dealt with in the future.

topicSummaries.topic: Climate Tort Bill Advances with Four-Week Select Committee Deadline
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill would prevent climate-related tort claims based on greenhouse-gas emissions, including the pending Smith v Fonterra proceedings, raising questions about access to courts and Parliament’s role.
topicSummaries.content: The Climate Change Response (Tort Liability) Amendment Bill passed its first reading and was referred to the Justice Committee, with a report due by 30 July 2026 and authority to meet outside normal sitting arrangements. The Government argued climate policy should be set by Parliament and the executive, rather than through case-by-case litigation. Labour and the Greens opposed the bill and challenged both its effect on existing proceedings and the short scrutiny period. Opposition amendments to extend the committee deadline were defeated.

keyExchanges.speaker: Paul Goldsmith (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The Government’s view is that greenhouse gas emissions and climate change harm are best regulated by Parliament and the executive.

keyExchanges.speaker: Steve Abel (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: It is a nullification of the right of citizens to exercise their equality before the law and hold those who are harming them accountable for the harm that has been caused.

topicSummaries.topic: Building Amendment Bill Referred for Scrutiny of Liability Reforms
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed changes could affect building costs, council liability, consumer protections and the speed of consent decisions.
topicSummaries.content: The Building Amendment Bill passed its first reading and was referred to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee. It proposes replacing joint and several liability with proportionate liability, introducing mandatory home warranties and professional indemnity insurance, easing collaboration between building consent authorities, and creating faster consent pathways for some sustainable homes and offsite-built granny flats. Labour supported referral but said its backing was conditional on scrutiny of insurance protections and the proposed changes to building research funding; the Greens raised concerns about relying on private insurance and moving research funding away from BRANZ.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Penk (National)
keyExchanges.quote: It makes a series of changes to improve efficiency, reduce delays, and ensure that responsibility and risk are allocated more fairly.

keyExchanges.speaker: Kieran McAnulty (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: We do want to support this. It is important that it has broad support.

topicSummaries.topic: Local Government Bill Advances as Parties Dispute Scope of Council Roles
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill changes the statutory focus of councils and could affect local decisions about services, community facilities and environmental work.
topicSummaries.content: The Local Government (System Improvements) Amendment Bill passed its second reading. The Government said it would refocus councils on infrastructure, public services and regulatory functions, while opposition MPs argued that removing the four wellbeings would narrow councils’ ability to support environmental, cultural and social initiatives. Labour also objected to proposed limits on committee voting rights for appointed members, including Māori representatives. The bill will proceed to its next stage in the House.

keyExchanges.speaker: Celia Wade-Brown (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: That’s not tidying up legislation; that’s setting up local government to fail.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tim Costley (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The National Party wants to see rates stop going up. We want to make them more affordable, and that’s why we’re refocusing the purpose of local government.

topicSummaries.topic: Primary Industries Regulatory Bill Passes After Technical Changes
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The omnibus law updates rules affecting farmers, growers, food producers and exporters, including biosecurity, levies and food standards.
topicSummaries.content: The Regulatory Systems (Primary Industries) Amendment Bill passed its third reading after changes across 19 Acts. The Government described the measures as technical updates to reduce administrative burdens and improve regulatory processes. Labour and the Greens supported the bill while raising questions about biosecurity powers, levy-setting, consultation and the scope for New Zealand food standards to differ from joint standards with Australia. The bill also enables fee relief for some horticulture exporters affected by severe weather and repeals several Acts whose transitional functions were described as complete.

conclusion: The Government secured passage or advancement of a broad legislative programme, while opposition concerns remained focused on whether fast-tracked reforms adequately protect rights, public services and communities.
